newsitem.title: GERMANY: Evacuees from Albania arrive in Germany.
newsitem.headline: Evacuees from Albania arrive in Germany.

text.p: Two planes carrying Germans and other nationals arrived in Germany on Friday after German soldiers rescued 120 people and airlifted them out of the Albanian capital, Tirana, in a spectacular operation.
Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel and Defence Minister Volker Ruehe as well as relatives and friends were waiting to greet them as the planes landed at Cologne military airport.

German soldiers opened fire under "hostile conditions" for the first time since World War Two, in the lightning operation to get 20 Germans and 100 others, mainly from European states, out of Albania, Ruehe told a news conference earlier.

Ruehe said he had sent in five military helicopters from Bosnia protected by 25 soldiers to fly the evacuees to Montenegro on Albania's northern border. Shortly afterwards they were taken on by plane to Germany.

German officials said some of the evacuees had stayed behind in Montenegro, including several Albanians who had managed to get on to the helicopters, and that over 100 people arrived in Germany representing a total of 22 nationalities.
The rescue operation took place as anarchy spread through the impoverished Balkan state to Tirana, with gunfire in the streets and widespread looting of armouries and food stores.
German military spokesmen Hartmut Bagger told the news conference gunmen started shooting at evacuees as the third of five German military helicopters landed, and the German soldiers fired back.

"We could hear a wild shoot-out without knowing where the gunshots came from, who was shooting at whom and what sort of weapons they were using," Bagger said, describing how he could hear the battle over the line as he spoke with the German ambassador by mobile telephone.

Bagger said a crowd of Albanians had tried to storm the helicopter and one of the German helicopters had been hit by gunfire. Bagger added that an Albanian had been lightly wounded but no foreigners were hurt.
Ruehe hailed the operation as a great success.

Kinkel told German ZDF television he was pleased that German troops had been able to help rescue citizens of other countries as well because, in the past, Germany had always been on the receiving end in such situations.
"I'm glad that we were able to carry out this operation for other countries, as they have done this for us in the past," Kinkel said.
The evacuees included 20 Danes, 13 Hungarians and 12 Austrians.
